flawed_step: Lines 0054-0067 (the 'If |R_{m-1}| < n/2' case): the proof pads R_{m-1} with arbitrary vertices of W_{m-1} to get |S| = n/2 and then asserts 'S is a subset of W_{m-1} with |S| = n/2 and crucially no neighbor in W_m (since S ⊇ R_{m-1} ...)', concluding N(S) ⊆ V \ W_m and |N(S)| ≤ αn. The containment runs the wrong way: only R_{m-1} is known to have no neighbor in W_m; the added vertices of S \ R_{m-1} lie in W_{m-1} \ R_{m-1}, which merely means they have no neighbor in R_{m-2}, and they may still be adjacent to many vertices of W_m. Line 0060's parenthetical 'no vertex in S lies in W_m (indeed S ⊆ W_{m-1})' additionally presumes W_{m-1} ∩ W_m = ∅, which is impossible here since |W_i| ≥ (1-α)n forces |W_{m-1} ∩ W_m| ≥ (1-2α)n.
counterexample: Concrete instance refuting the proof's inference 'R_{m-1} ⊆ S ⊆ W_{m-1} and R_{m-1} has no neighbor in W_m  ⇒  N(S) ⊆ V \ W_m and |N(S)| ≤ αn'. Take n = 20, α = 1/5 (so n/2 = 10, αn = 4, (1-α)n = 16), V = {1,...,20}, k = 4. Edges of G (13 of them): 1-19, 2-19, 3-19, 4-19, 5-19, 6-19, 7-19, 8-19, 11-17, 12-17, 13-17, 14-18, 15-18; vertices 9, 10, 16, 20 isolated. Sets: W1 = {1,...,16} (|W1| = 16), W2 = V \ {17,18} (18), W3 = V \ {19,20} = {1,...,18} (18), W4 = V \ {19,20} = {1,...,18} (18); all sizes ≥ 16 = (1-α)n. Run the proof's own BFS: R1 = W1 = {1,...,16}. N(R1) = {17,18,19} (17 via 11,12,13; 18 via 14,15; 19 via 1..8), so R2 = N(R1) ∩ W2 = {19} (17,18 ∉ W2), nonempty. N(R2) = N(19) = {1,...,8}, so R3 = N(R2) ∩ W3 = {1,...,8}, nonempty. N(R3) = {19}, and 19 ∉ W4, so R4 = N(R3) ∩ W4 = ∅. Hence m = 4, R3 = {1,...,8} is nonempty with no neighbor in W4 (its only neighbor is 19 ∉ W4) — exactly the configuration the proof handles. Since |R3| = 8 < n/2 = 10, the proof instructs: extend R3 to S with R3 ⊆ S ⊆ W3 and |S| = n/2. A legitimate such choice is S = {1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,17,18} (17,18 ∈ W3, |S| = 10). The proof now asserts N(S) ⊆ V \ W4 = {19,20} and |N(S)| ≤ αn = 4. In fact N(S) = N({1..8}) ∪ N({17,18}) = {19} ∪ {11,12,13,14,15} = {11,12,13,14,15,19}: it contains 11,12,13,14,15 ∈ W4, so N(S) ⊈ V \ W4, and |N(S)| = 6 > 4 = αn. Both the containment and the numeric bound the proof needs fail, so no contradiction with the expansion hypothesis is produced. (This graph of course violates the expansion hypothesis — it must, since the theorem itself is true — but the proof's step is presented as a general deduction from 'R_{m-1} ⊆ S ⊆ W_{m-1}, R_{m-1} has no neighbor in W_m', and that deduction is what the instance refutes: the padding vertices 17,18 ∈ W3 \ R3 carry 5 neighbors inside W4.)
reasoning_summary: The base case (k = 2) is sound. The inductive/BFS argument is not. Everything hinges on producing a set S of size exactly n/2 with |N(S)| ≤ αn. The proof gets this only for R_{m-1}, the reachable set at the last nonempty layer, which genuinely has no neighbor in W_m. When |R_{m-1}| < n/2 the proof pads S up to size n/2 with arbitrary vertices of W_{m-1} and then claims the no-neighbors-in-W_m property still holds 'since S ⊇ R_{m-1}' — monotonicity in the wrong direction. A vertex u ∈ W_{m-1} \ R_{m-1} is unreachable only because it has no neighbor in R_{m-2}; nothing stops u from having many neighbors in W_m. The supporting remark that no vertex of S lies in W_m 'indeed S ⊆ W_{m-1}' is also false, since consecutive W_i overlap in at least (1-2α)n vertices. I built an explicit 20-vertex, 13-edge instance with α = 1/5 and k = 4 in which the proof's own BFS yields m = 4, R3 = {1,...,8} with no neighbor in W4, and the sanctioned padded set S = {1..8,17,18} has N(S) = {11,...,15,19} of size 6 > αn = 4 and meeting W4. So the claimed contradiction does not follow and the proof of the inductive step is invalid as written.
